relation_kind: tension

basis: "The Apology asserts a substantive thesis about what virtue does (it generates money and all other human goods). The Meno claims Socrates does not know what virtue itself is and argues that without knowing what something is, one cannot know what sort of thing it is. If the Meno's priority-of-definition rule is applied rigorously, then the Apology thesis could not be asserted with knowledge. The two claims pull against one another: one makes a positive claim about virtue's effects, the other denies knowledge of virtue's essence and by implication of its properties."
limits: "The tension is between the epistemic stance in the Meno and the substantive thesis in the Apology. Both claims are left standing in their respective dialogues. This relation does not resolve whether the Apology thesis could be held as a practical exhortation without claiming definitional knowledge, nor does it address whether the Meno's priority rule applies to all knowledge or only to definitional inquiry."

```

relation_kind: tension
resolution: standing
basis: "The Apology claim treats virtue as real and causally efficacious (generative of goods). The Phaedo claim is a reductio: if soul is a harmony, then virtue (as harmony) and vice (as disharmony) would be properties of soul-as-harmony, and the absurd conclusion would follow that no soul can participate in vice. The Phaedo claim uses ἀρετή within a hypothetical framework being refuted, so it does not directly contradict the Apology claim, but the Phaedo's dialectical use of 'virtue as harmony' implicitly raises a question about what virtue is — and whether the Apology's confidence in virtue's effects presupposes an answer that the Phaedo's harmony hypothesis would challenge."
limits: "The Phaedo claim is part of a reductio ad absurdum of the harmony hypothesis; it does not itself assert a positive thesis about virtue. The tension exists at the level of how ἀρετή is treated across the two dialogues: as an unproblematic given in the Apology, and as a term embedded in a refuted hypothesis in the Phaedo. This relation does not claim that the Apology thesis is invalidated by the Phaedo argument."
review_status: accepted
```

limits: "The Protagoras claim is presented by Socrates as Protagoras's position, not as Socrates's own view. The Apology claim is Socrates's own exhortation. ```yaml
relation_id: rel_cross-dialogue_0021
pair_id: pair_cross-dialogue_00021
claim_a: claim_charmides_0014
claim_b: claim_phaedrus_0030
relation_kind: contradiction
resolution: standing
basis: "The Charmides defines σωφροσύνη as the doing of good things — a positive moral quality. The Phaedrus presents σωφροσύνη as what the former lover changes to (from eros and madness), and in that state he becomes untrustworthy: he flees from his promises and harms his former beloved. In the Phaedrus, the lover who turns to σωφροσύνη is the villain, not the benefactor. If σωφροσύνη is doing good things (Charmides), then the σώφρων ex-lover who breaks promises and abandons the beloved is contradicting the definition. The two claims cannot both stand as stated without additional qualification about what counts as 'good things' in the erotic context."
limits: "Both claims are left standing. The Phaedrus claim is the conclusion of Socrates's first speech delivered in the character of the non-lover — it may not represent Socrates's own view. The contradiction is between the Charmides definition and the non-lover's position in the Phaedrus, not necessarily between Socrates's positions in the two dialogues. A verbal resolution might be available if 'good things' in the Charmides definition is specified further, but no such specification is present in either claim as recorded."
review_status: accepted
```

limits: "Both claims are left_standing. The Charmides definition is Critias's proposal under examination. The Republic thesis is asserted in the philosopher-nature discussion. Neither text addresses the other's framing."
review_status: accepted
```

Both passages deploy the same conceptual move — a single knowledge that encompasses its own scope — and both are left standing as theses. The Charmides formulation is the more reflexive version (knowledge taking itself as object), while the Laches formulation addresses temporal unification, but the underlying epistemic architecture is the same: epistēmē is comprehensive and self-contained rather than fragmented."
limits: "This does not claim that the Laches passage is about sōphrosynē or that Critias endorses Socrates's temporal thesis. The relation is limited to the shared structural claim about the unity and reflexivity of epistēmē."
review_status: accepted
```

basis: "Charmides 172a reports that no reflexive knowledge (knowledge of what one knows and does not know) has appeared anywhere, treating the search as a failure. The Republic passage supplies the object-based differentiation that the Charmides investigation could not find. By distinguishing epistēmē-simpliciter from qualified epistēmai, Republic 438c-438e offers a framework in which a second-order knowledge could be conceptualized as a qualified epistēmē whose object is epistēmē itself. This is a substantive advance over the Charmides passage's negative conclusion."
limits: "This does not claim that Republic 438c-438e was written to resolve the Charmides aporia, nor that the Republic passage explicitly endorses a reflexive knowledge. It only notes that the Republic taxonomy provides conceptual resources not available in the Charmides passage."
review_status: accepted
```

The two uses of ψυχή point in different directions — one physiological, one ethical — without formal contradiction."

review_status: accepted
```

The tension is subtle: the Cratylus definition makes obstruction intrinsic to what κακόν is, while Republic treats an evil as proper (οἰκεῖον) or alien (ἀλλότριον) to a thing."
limits: "Both claims are left standing. The Cratylus etymology does not address the proper/alien distinction, and the Republic does not address etymology. Not a formal contradiction."
review_status: accepted
```

The Meno passage merely includes σοφία in an enumerative list of virtues; it says nothing about σοφία's relationship to good fortune or its infallibility. The Euthydemus passage makes a substantive claim about σοφία that goes far beyond the bare enumeration in Meno. The two claims share the inclusion of σοφία as a positive item but differ in ambition."
limits: "The shared term σοφία appears in both as something valued, but the Meno passage treats it as one virtue among many while the Euthydemus passage makes it the decisive factor in good fortune. Both claims are left_standing. Not a genuine restatement because the claims differ in content and argumentative function."
review_status: rejected
```

basis: "Euthyphro claim_a offers a specific definition of holiness as epistêmê of asking and giving to the gods — implying that epistêmê can be specified in content. Theaetetus claim_b records Socrates' avowed aporia: he cannot adequately grasp what epistêmê itself is (ἐπιστήμη ὅτι ποτὲ τυγχάνει ὄν, 145e). A tension arises because in Euthyphro epistêmê is used as an unproblematic genus-term in a definition of holiness, while in Theaetetus the very nature of epistêmê is presented as unknown and the subject of aporia."
limits: "The Euthyphro definition is drawn from Euthyphro's conceded premises and posed for examination, not Socrates' own settled view. The Theaetetus aporia is an avowal that may be ironic or heuristic. The tension is between using epistêmê as a definitional tool and questioning its very nature, but the two claims belong to different dramatic and dialectical contexts and do not formally contradict."
review_status: accepted
```

```yaml
relation_id: rel_cross-dialogue_0253
pair_id: pair_cross-dialogue_00253
claim_a: claim_euthyphro_0043
claim_b: claim_theaetetus_0005
relation_kind: tension
resolution: superseded
basis: >
  Both claims use epistēmē as their genus term, but in incompatible structural directions. In Euthyphro 14c-14d, epistēmē appears as the genus of holiness: holiness is knowledge of a specific transactional domain (asking and giving to the gods). The definiendum is holiness, and epistēmē serves as the higher-order category under which a specific divine-human exchange practice falls. In Theaetetus 146c-146d, epistēmē is the definiendum itself: Theaetetus lists geometry, shoemaking, and other crafts as instances of epistēmē, treating crafts as species falling under epistēmē. The two claims share the term epistēmē but deploy it at opposite levels of the genus-species hierarchy: in the Euthyphro claim epistēmē is the container, in the Theaetetus claim epistēmē is what the crafts collectively are. They are not contradictory because the hierarchy reversal does not produce a formal logical conflict absent further premises; they are in tension because the same term is being used in structurally opposite definitional roles without reconciliation.
limits: >
  This record does not assess whether the Euthyphro's transactional epistēmē could be harmonized with the Theaetetus's crafts-as-epistēmē, nor whether either speaker would endorse the other's usage. Both claims are left standing in their respective dialogues; the tension is in their structural deployment of the shared term.
  Resolution updated from standing to superseded on 2026-07-12 by the claim-fate pilot Phase 2 after operator-authorized stance-event threading changed claim_theaetetus_0005 to final_status revised; prose above describes the pre-threading state.

```yaml
relation_id: rel_cross-dialogue_0273
pair_id: pair_cross-dialogue_00273
claim_a: claim_gorgias_0038
claim_b: claim_laws_0764
relation_kind: contradiction
resolution: standing
basis: >
  Both claims concern the relation between rhetoric (or civic activity) and crafts (δημιουργοί). In the Gorgias claim, Gorgias asserts that with rhetoric alone one is in no way inferior to the craftsmen (δημιουργῶν) without learning the other crafts. In the Laws claim, the Athenian asserts that no citizen shall practice a craft, that no human nature can practice two arts with precision, and that the citizen already has a sufficient art in preserving the common order. These claims contradict each other on the question of whether a non-craft pursuit (rhetoric in Gorgias, civic order in Laws) can make one equal or superior to craftsmen: Gorgias says yes, rhetoric alone suffices to be not inferior to craftsmen; the Laws says the citizen's civic art is itself exclusive of craft-practice, implying that mastery of one art excludes competence in others, whereas Gorgias suggests rhetorical mastery compensates for ignorance of crafts.
limits: >
  Gorgias' claim is presented as an attractive feature of rhetoric he has not secured by argument, and the Laws claim is a legislative prescription, not a descriptive thesis. The contradiction is between the claims as stated in the texts, not between demonstrated doctrines. The record does not claim that Plato intended the Laws to refute Gorgias.
review_status: accepted
```

But the Gorgias claim concerns a moral conclusion about justice, while the Republic claim concerns a craft-norm about competition among fellow practitioners. They do not address the same subject and are not in formal contradiction."
limits: "The relation identifies a shared argumentative structure—a necessity conclusion derived from craft-based premises—without claiming that the two passages are about the same thing or that one constrains the other."
review_status: accepted
```

Greater Hippias 283e-284a asserts that in well-governed cities virtue is held in highest honor (τιμιώτατον) — a claim about the normative valuation of virtue within an established polity. Laws 678a-678b makes a genetic claim that virtue and wickedness emerged together with cities, constitutions, crafts, and laws from post-catastrophe conditions — a claim about the historical co-origination of virtue with political institutions. These are not contradictory as stated: one can hold that virtue arises historically alongside political forms and also that well-governed cities subsequently honor it most highly. The tension lies in the different registers: one is synchronic and evaluative (virtue's honor in functioning cities), the other is diachronic and developmental (virtue's emergence from pre-political conditions). Neither claim has been refuted, withdrawn, or revised."
limits: "This pair does not establish that Plato held a single doctrine of virtue's relation to the polis. The two passages belong to different dialogues with different interlocutors, dramatic contexts, and argumentative purposes. No causal or logical entailment between the two claims is asserted here."
review_status: rejected
```

review_status: accepted

The Republic passage (395c) says guardians, as precise craftsmen of the city's freedom, must imitate only what befits them from childhood: courage, moderation, piety, freedom, and must not imitate what is slavish or shameful. The shared term μιμεῖσθαι and the shared structure of imitation-toward-virtue create a real thematic link. However, the target of imitation differs: the Laws points to a mythic divine age, while Republic points to virtues appropriate to guardian-craftsmen. The Athenian's claim is universal (all of us must imitate), while the Republic claim is restricted to a specific class under a specific hypothesis. These differences produce a pull rather than a formal contradiction."
limits: "This record does not claim the two dialogues share a unified doctrine of imitation. It does not assess whether the Republic's guardian-restriction is compatible with the Laws' universal prescription. The relation is confined to the textual observation that both passages use μιμεῖσθαι to prescribe imitation toward a normative ethical model, with different scopes and targets."
review_status: accepted
```

Both claims treat σωφροσύνη as a normative standard that should hold the superior rank in a value hierarchy. The Laws passage ranks temperance above health and health above wealth in correct legislation; the Symposium passage ranks temperance (embodied by Eros) above all other pleasures. The shared formal structure is: temperance occupies the top of an evaluative ranking, and a state of affairs where something else outranks temperance is corrupt or impossible. There is no contradiction because the two claims address different domains (political constitution versus erotic psychology) and different speakers (Athenian Stranger versus Agathon), but the same conceptual pattern of temperance-as-supreme-ranking-standard recurs."
limits: "This relation records a formal restatement of the temperance-ranking pattern across dialogues. It does not claim that the Athenian Stranger and Agathon share the same doctrine, that one dialogue depends on the other, or that Plato endorses either speaker's position. Both claims are left standing in their respective contexts, and no resolving span is cited."
review_status: accepted
```

Both passages treat ἀνελευθερία as a term of ethical condemnation, but the Laws passage treats it as a genuine vice to be removed, while the Republic passage treats it as a slander directed at a genuine virtue. These are compatible: one work describes illiberality as a real impediment to wisdom; the other describes the same term being used deceptively to attack measured expenditure."
limits: "This tension does not constitute a contradiction because the two claims address different speakers, different argumentative functions, and opposite valences of the term ἀνελευθερία (vice-to-be-cured vs. slander-against-virtue). basis: "Both claims address γελοῖον (the ridiculous) and its relationship to seriousness, but they make distinct, non-identical claims. Republic 452d-e asserts that the ridiculous is only the bad (τὸ κακόν) and that anyone who aims laughter at anything other than the foolish and bad is empty. Laws 935a-b asserts that habitually engaging in ridicule of an opponent causes one to miss seriousness (σπουδαίου τρόπου) or lose parts of high-mindedness (μεγαλονοίας). Republic defines the proper object of laughter; Laws describes the corrupting effect of habitual ridicule on the speaker. The claims are compatible — one can consistently hold both that ridicule should target only the bad and that habitual ridicule corrupts seriousness — but the different emphases (normative definition vs. psychological consequence) and distinct contexts create a pull: Republic limits what qualifies as legitimate ridicule, while Laws warns that even engaging in ridicule at all risks moral damage, which implicitly questions whether the Republic's sanctioned ridicule is psychologically sustainable."
limits: "The two claims are not formally contradictory because Republic does not assert that habitual ridicule is safe, and Laws does not assert that the ridiculous is not the bad. The tension is between Republic's permissive framing (ridicule of the bad is proper) and Laws' cautionary framing (habitual ridicule invariably damages seriousness and high-mindedness). Whether Laws 935a-b would judge even Republic's normatively proper ridicule as corrupting is not resolved in either passage. Both claims have final_status left_standing."
review_status: accepted
```

The difference in framing (virtue-with-wisdom vs. definition-as-rational-rule) creates pull without contradiction."
limits: "This record does not assess whether the two dialogues share a consistent theory of σωφροσύνη. The claims occupy different argumentative contexts and domains (physiology vs. psychology/ethics) and neither is staked on the other."
limits: "This relation is limited to the observation that both claims deploy the concept of an οἰκεῖον property or cause, in each case to distinguish what properly belongs to a thing from what does not. The relation does not assert that the two passages share a common theory of causation, nor does it establish any direct influence or reference. The Phaedo passage is explicitly marked as a former belief Socrates no longer holds, which further limits any claim of doctrinal consistency or conflict."
review_status: accepted
```

In Republic 452d–452e the claim is that the ridiculous (γελοῖον) is nothing other than the bad (κακόν), and the serious effort toward the noble aims only at the good (ἀγαθοῦ). In Statesman 296c the Visitor asks whether the error contrary to the political art is the shameful (αἰσχρὸν), the bad (κακόν), and the unjust (ἄδικον), which the Younger Socrates affirms. Both passages treat κακόν as the proper object of a negative stance — ridicule in the Republic, art-error in the Statesman — and link it to further negative predicates. The Republic passage adds the foolish (ἄφρων) and the good (ἀγαθόν) as the contrasting positive term, while the Statesman adds the shameful and the unjust, but the core identification of the bad as the target of a negative evaluative attitude is common to both.

The Statesman passage ties the claim specifically to political art error, while the Republic passage ties it to the ridiculous and the serious. The two claims deploy the same structure (κακόν as the proper object of a negative normative response) in different argument contexts.
review_status: accepted
```

basis: Both claims address how the soul grasps normative pairs (good/bad, fine/shameful) and share the Greek term κακόν. In Republic 452d-452e, the thesis asserts that the ridiculous (γελοῖον) is only the bad (κακόν) and that one who looks to any other appearance as ridiculous than that of the foolish and bad is empty. This is a prescriptive claim about the proper object of laughter and seriousness, tying the ridiculous exclusively to the bad. In Theaetetus 186a-186b, the soul is said to examine the being (οὐσίαν) of like, unlike, same, different, and especially of fine and shameful and good and bad (καλὸν καὶ αἰσχρὸν καὶ ἀγαθὸν καὶ κακόν), reckoning past and present in relation to future. This is a descriptive claim about the soul's cognitive access to normative kinds. The two claims pull in different directions: Republic ties the ridiculous to a normative evaluation of the bad, while Theaetetus treats good and bad as objects of the soul's reflective examination without any reference to the ridiculous. They are not formally contradictory because they address different domains (comedy and seriousness versus the soul's cognitive capacity), but the shared vocabulary of κακόν/κακὸν and the normative register create a pull between a prescriptive cultural claim and a descriptive epistemological one.
limits: This relation is limited to the shared term κακόν and the common concern with how good and bad are grasped. The claims operate in different argumentative contexts (education and culture in Republic, epistemology in Theaetetus) and do not directly engage the same thesis. The tension is one of register and framing rather than logical incompatibility.
review_status: accepted
```

Republic 573b describes the erotic 'protector of the soul' purging moderation (σωφροσύνη) to fill the soul with imported madness—a destructive inward process. Symposium 216d presents Socrates as concealing deep σωφροσύνη inside an outwardly erotic, ignorant satyr-figure—an inward possession. The claims are not formally contradictory: one is a portrait of tyrannical-eros-as-disease expelling moderation, the other a portrait of Socratic-eros-as-container concealing moderation. But they pull against each other on whether eros is compatible with inward σωφροσύνη."
limits: "This relation is limited to the textual compatibility of the two claim contents as stated. It does not adjudicate whether the Symposium portrait is Alcibiades' or Socrates' own view, nor whether Republic 573b is endorsed by the dialogue's Socrates. The two works are not in the same argumentative frame; one is descriptive psychology of the tyrannical man, the other is encomiastic portraiture."
review_status: accepted
```

In both passages, the term εἶδος names the unitary entity that is generated-from-yet-distinct-from a plurality, and in both the argument turns on the claim that the composite cannot be reduced to its constituents without losing the unity. The Republic passage uses the couch as an illustrative vehicle for the form-uniqueness argument; the Theaetetus passage applies the same structural move to the syllable-elements problem. The Theaetetus claim is marked revised at 203e relative to its own dialogue context, not relative to the Republic passage. Since the Theaetetus passage revises an earlier position within its own dialogue and the shared pattern is structural rather than a chain of doctrinal revision, the closest narrow resolution is superseded."
limits: "This identifies a shared form-language structure and argument pattern, not a direct intertextual reference. In Theaetetus 171a Socrates draws the dialectical consequence that Protagoras must concede his contradictors speak truly when they opine what is (τὰ ὄντα), since he holds all opinion is of what is. The Sophist passage works out a formal definition of false statement in terms of being and not-being, while the Theaetetus passage uses the same ontological vocabulary to expose a self-refutation in Protagoras's measure doctrine. They pull in the same conceptual direction but operate in different argumentative contexts and do not make formally contradictory or identical claims.
limits: This relation records a shared conceptual vocabulary (τὰ ὄντα / what is) used in two distinct dialectical contexts, not a formal restatement or revision. The Sophist definition is a constructive Eleatic account of true and false logos; the Theaetetus passage is a reductio ad absurdum of Protagorean relativism. Whether the Theaetetus argument presupposes or anticipates the Sophist account of not-being is not adjudicated here.
review_status: accepted
```

The Theaetetus claim operates within the syllable-element analysis and states a conditional: if the syllable has no parts and is a single form (μία ἰδέα), then it falls into the same form (εἶδος) as the element. The Statesman claim is a general taxonomic principle about the relationship between species and part; the Theaetetus claim is a conditional about what happens when a composite (syllable) lacks parts. Both claims are left standing in their respective dialogues. They pull against each other insofar as the Statesman insists on a species/part distinction, while the Theaetetus scenario contemplates a case where a putative composite is partless and thus shares the form of its elements — but the Theaetetus claim is explicitly conditional and does not assert that any syllable actually is partless, so no formal contradiction arises."
limits: "This record does not establish that Plato holds a unified theory of εἶδος across dialogues. It notes only that two claims sharing the term εἶδος address part-whole relations in different argumentative settings without formal contradiction. The Theaetetus claim is conditional; the Statesman claim defers full treatment to a later occasion."
review_status: accepted
```

Statesman 296d-296e makes the wise-and-good man's administration for the benefit of the ruled the truest standard of correct city-administration, independent of external markers like wealth or written law. Timaeus 88c-88d makes rightly being called καλός τε καὶ ἀγαθός depend on reciprocal care of body and soul, refusing to separate intellectual and physical cultivation. The shared term ἀγαθός functions as the unifying predicate in structurally parallel formulations: each claim defines the condition under which someone or something is correctly judged to meet the standard of goodness. Neither claim restricts ἀγαθός to a single domain; the Statesman claim applies it to the ruler's character as the grounding of correct rule, and the Timaeus claim applies it to the individual's balanced cultivation. The claims do not contradict, revise, or stand in tension; they articulate compatible aspects of what it means to be ἀγαθός — one political, one anthropological — without overlapping in the specific conditions they prescribe."
limits: "The claims share the term ἀγαθός but address different domains (political rule vs. individual self-cultivation). This relation records a structural and terminological restatement, not an identity of doctrinal content. Whether the Statesman's wise-and-good ruler must also satisfy the Timaeus's balance of body and soul is not addressed in either passage."
review_status: accepted
```

Timaeus 37e-38a makes a different point: only 'is' (estin) properly belongs to eternal being (aidion ousian), while 'was' and 'will be' belong to generation in time. The Theaetetus passage does not make a claim about temporal predication, and the Timaeus passage does not deny that the soul can reach after ousia. The term ousia appears in both but the claims operate on different planes: one concerns epistemic access, the other concerns the grammar of temporal predication."
limits: "No formal contradiction, since neither claim denies what the other asserts. The Theaetetus claim does not specify whether the soul's grasp of ousia involves temporal language, and the Timaeus claim does not address how the soul accesses eternal being. A tension remains in that Timaeus restricts what can be properly said of eternal ousia, while Theaetetus presents the soul as reaching out after ousia without addressing these restrictions. Whether the two accounts are ultimately compatible depends on claims neither text makes here."
review_status: accepted
```
